transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Dubois, Mrs. Dubois, thank you for sitting down with me. I need to discuss something that happened during your scan this morning. There was a medical error. We gave you the contrast dye despite your blood tests showing that your kidney function was too low to safely handle it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Normally, when the creatinine level in the blood is as high as yours, we have to follow a special protocol to protect the kidneys before giving the dye. That protocol was not followed, and the dye was administered anyway. Does that make sense, or can I explain that differently?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I do not understand. You told me the scan was fine. Now you tell me you have damaged my kidneys?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is possible that the dye has caused an injury to your kidneys, which we call contrast nephropathy. To make sure I'm being clear, are you asking if the damage is permanent or if it has happened already?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Both! Why would this happen?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It happened because the check for kidney function was missed before the injection. This was a failure in the process of care.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: C'est inadmissible! I come here and I trust you, and you treat me like a number! I am not a number!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like you feel completely disregarded, and that your dignity hasn't been respected.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am a grown man. I have lived my life with pride. To be told you were a mistake, a clerical error... it is insulting.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see how deeply wounding this is for you. To feel that your care was handled carelessly is an incredibly painful experience.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And now? What happens to my kidneys? Who is responsible for this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The team failed to follow the safety protocol. It was an oversight in the administration of the contrast.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are not saying it. Say it. Who did this?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The protocol was not performed. The dye was given when it should not have been.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You are speaking in circles. I want to know if you are sorry.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are working to monitor your levels now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I do not care about the monitoring! I am asking if you are sorry for this mistake!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The system for flagging kidney function didn't trigger the alert.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I am talking to you, not the system!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand this is frustrating.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Frustrating? My health is at risk because someone was lazy!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear how angry you are, and you have every right to be. It is frightening to think your health was put at risk because a safety step was missed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I cannot believe this. I feel... I feel cheated.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Being cheated of the care you expected and deserved is a terrible feeling. I am here with you now, and we are going to focus entirely on your recovery.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What is the plan then? Because I do not trust you to just "monitor" me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I have a very specific plan to manage this. First, I have already started you on an intravenous saline drip. This will help flush the dye out of your system and protect the kidneys. This is running right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: For how long?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We will keep the fluids running for the next twenty-four hours. Second, we are going to draw your blood every twelve hours—starting at 6 PM tonight—to check your creatinine levels and see exactly how your kidneys are responding.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And if the numbers stay high?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: If the levels do not improve by tomorrow morning, I will bring in the nephrologist, our kidney specialist, for a formal consultation at 9 AM.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do I have to do? I am just lying here.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Your role is to let us know immediately if you notice any decrease in how much you are urinating or if you feel any new swelling in your ankles. That is the most important signal you can give us.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I will watch. I have no choice.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it feels that way. Regarding how this happened, I am documenting this as a sentinel event. This means the hospital leadership will review the chart to figure out why the alert failed so that this cannot happen to another patient.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That does not fix my kidneys.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, it doesn't. But it is the step we take to ensure this error is not repeated. I will be back in one hour to check your drip and speak with you again. Does that timeline work for you?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I suppose.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will see you shortly.

H.justification: The resident never interrupts the patient, remains regulated despite significant pushback, and allows the patient to express anger and frustration without rushing.

E.justification: The error is named in the first turn, lay language is used throughout, and comprehension is checked twice ('Does that make sense', 'are you asking if...').

A.justification: The resident never uses direct apology language ('I'm sorry' or 'I apologize') and deflects responsibility to 'the process of care' and 'the system' when asked directly.

R.justification: The resident names specific emotions ('disregarded', 'wounding', 'angry', 'cheated') and engages directly with the patient's emotional bids.

T.justification: The plan includes specific steps (saline drip, blood draws), clear timelines (24 hours, 6 PM, 9 AM), a named patient role (monitoring urine/swelling), and a prevention step (sentinel event documentation).
